slides.title: Before the Finnish Civil War
slides.body: Finland's independence from Russia coincided with food shortages, social polarization, armed militias, and the revolutionary crisis created by World War I.

stats.lbl: The Red and White camps fought over political power, social order, and the future direction of the new Finnish state.

markers.label: Åland Islands

markers.label: Mariehamn

slides.title: Invasion of Åland
slides.body: The Invasion of Åland was a 1918 military campaign of World War I in Åland, Finland. The islands, still hosting Soviet Russian troops, were first invaded by Sweden in late February and then by the German Empire in early March. The conflict was also related to the Finnish Civil War including minor fighting between the Finnish Whites and the Finnish Reds.

stats.lbl: The Invasion of Åland was a 1918 military campaign of World War I in Åland, Finland.

markers.label: Tampere
markers.description: The decisive urban battle broke Red power in inland Finland.

markers.label: Kalevankangas
markers.description: A prison camp and execution site after the battle.

slides.title: Battle of Tampere
slides.body: The Battle of Tampere was a 1918 Finnish Civil War battle, fought in Tampere, Finland from 15 March to 6 April between the Whites and the Reds. It is the most famous and deadly of all the Finnish Civil War battles. Its bloody aftermath saw the Whites execute hundreds of captured Reds with another 11,000 prisoners sent to the Kalevankangas camp.

stats.lbl: The Battle of Tampere was a 1918 Finnish Civil War battle, fought in Tampere, Finland from 15 March to 6 April between the Whites and the Reds.

markers.label: Ruovesi

slides.title: Battle of Ruovesi
slides.body: The Battle of Ruovesi was a major battle during the Finnish Civil War and on the Eastern Front of World War I fought in Ruovesi, Finland from 5 February to 19 March 1918 between the Whites and the Reds with support for the latter from Russian volunteers.

stats.lbl: The Battle of Ruovesi was a major battle during the Finnish Civil War and on the Eastern Front of World War I fought in Ruovesi, Finland from 5 February to 19 March 1918 between the Whites and the Reds with support for the latter from Russian volunteers.

slides.title: Battle of Rautu
slides.body: The Battle of Rautu was a 1918 Finnish Civil War battle, fought in Rautu, Finland from 21 February to 5 April 1918 between the Finnish Whites and the Finnish Reds supported by the Russian Bolsheviks.

markers.label: Helsinki
markers.description: German troops and Finnish Whites captured the Red-held capital in April 1918.

markers.label: Harbor approaches
markers.description: German forces used the coast and city approaches in the assault.

slides.title: Battle of Helsinki
slides.body: The Battle of Helsinki was a 1918 Finnish Civil War battle, fought on 12–13 April by the German troops and Finnish Whites against the Finnish Reds in Helsinki, Finland. Together with the battles of Tampere and Vyborg, it was one of the three major urban battles of the Finnish Civil War. The Germans invaded Helsinki despite the opposition of Finnish White Army leader Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim who wanted to attack the capital city with his own troops after Tampere had fallen on 6 April. However, the Germans had their own interest in taking Helsinki as quickly as possible and then moving further east towards the Russian border. The city had been under Red control for 11 weeks since the beginning of the war.

slides.title: The Wider Impact
slides.body:
The Red and White camps fought over political power, social order, and the future direction of the new Finnish state.

Consequences: The effects of Battle of Helsinki extended beyond its immediate result. Executions, prison camps, hunger, and political terror killed many people after the largest battles had ended.

stats.lbl: The Battle of Helsinki was a 1918 Finnish Civil War battle, fought on 12–13 April by the German troops and Finnish Whites against the Finnish Reds in Helsinki, Finland.

markers.label: Viipuri
markers.description: The battle captured a major Red stronghold near the end of the war.

slides.title: Battle of Viipuri
slides.body: The Battle of Viipuri was a 1918 Finnish Civil War battle, fought 24–29 April between the Finnish Whites and the Finnish Reds in Viipuri. Together with the Battle of Tampere and Battle of Helsinki, it was one of the three major urban battles of the Finnish Civil War. The battle is also remembered because of its bloody aftermath, as the Whites executed up to 400 non-aligned military personnel and civilians of Russian and associated ethnicities.

stats.lbl: The Battle of Viipuri was a 1918 Finnish Civil War battle, fought 24–29 April between the Finnish Whites and the Finnish Reds in Viipuri.

markers.label: Hämeenlinna
markers.description: White forces captured this city as Red resistance collapsed.

slides.title: Battle of Hämeenlinna
slides.body: The Battle of Hämeenlinna was a battle within the Finnish Civil War that took place in the city of Hämeenlinna, Finland on 26 April 1918.

stats.lbl: The Battle of Hämeenlinna was a battle within the Finnish Civil War that took place in the city of Hämeenlinna, Finland on 26 April 1918.

markers.label: Viipuri/Vyborg
markers.description: White Guards killed hundreds of Russians and suspected Reds during and after the city's capture.

slides.title: Vyborg massacre
slides.body: The Viipuri massacre was the killing of approximately 360 to 420 Russians in the city of Viipuri during the Finnish Civil War in April–May 1918. The massacre took place during and after the Battle of Viipuri as the White Guards captured the city from the Red Guards. At least half of the victims were Russian soldiers and military personnel. The slain were mainly men and young boys, as young as 12-13 years old: nine out of ten were men fit for military service, according to Finnish propaganda. The White Guards were "cleansing" the city of Red Guards of whom 800 were slain; however, only a small minority of the killed Russians were affiliated with the Finnish labour movement.

slides.title: The Wider Impact
slides.body:
The Red and White camps fought over political power, social order, and the future direction of the new Finnish state.

Consequences: The effects of Vyborg massacre extended beyond its immediate result. Executions, prison camps, hunger, and political terror killed many people after the largest battles had ended.

title: International and Human Dimensions
sub: The wider impact of the Finnish Civil War

markers.label: German intervention
markers.description: German troops helped capture Helsinki and shaped the war's final phase.

markers.label: Prison camps
markers.description: Executions, hunger, and disease in camps made the aftermath especially deadly.

markers.label: Russian collapse
markers.description: Russia's revolution and retreat created the space in which Finland's internal conflict exploded.

slides.title: International Dimension
slides.body:
German troops supported the Whites, while Russian forces and the wider revolutionary struggle influenced the Reds.

The Human Cost: Executions, prison camps, hunger, and political terror killed many people after the largest battles had ended.

title: Outcome and Legacy
sub: How the Finnish Civil War ended and what followed

markers.label: Helsinki
markers.description: The capital returned to White control, but the country emerged traumatized and divided.

markers.label: Tampere
markers.description: The battle became the central symbol of the war's violence.

markers.label: Viipuri
markers.description: The final phase left a bitter legacy of reprisals and ethnic violence.

slides.title: The End of the Finnish Civil War
slides.body: The White victory secured a non-socialist government but left deep divisions that shaped Finnish politics for decades.
